result: Deletion of mreB from P. fluorescens SBW25 produces viable spherical cells with increased and variable cell volume, reduced fitness, and altered growth characteristics compared to wild-type cells.
evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C18 are well-supported by microscopy (Figure 1A-B), cell volume measurements, flow cytometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1-2), fitness assays (Figure 1C), and growth curves (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Complementation experiments (C18) confirm causality. The data consistently demonstrate that ΔmreB cells are viable but compromised.

result: ΔmreB cells maintain an elongation axis that rotates 90° after division, with septum formation perpendicular to this axis, and exhibit elongation rates indistinguishable from wild-type during exponential phase.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by time-lapse microscopy showing aspect ratio measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 5-6, Video 1) and elongation rate data (Figure 1D). The observation that elongation rates are unchanged despite morphological changes is surprising but well-documented.

result: The reduced fitness of ΔmreB mutants is primarily due to decreased cell viability (81% vs 95% for wild-type), with probability of producing offspring (p=0.85) consistent between single-cell and bulk measurements.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by live/dead assays (Figure 1E), time-lapse microscopy measurements, and statistical comparison between single-cell (p=0.85±0.05) and bulk fitness (0.77±0.025) experiments. The consistency between methods strengthens the conclusion.

result: ΔmreB cells exhibit significant defects in septum positioning accuracy (19.4% vs 5% volume difference in sister cells) and growth asymmetry between sister cells (55% vs 5% difference in elongation rate), leading to variable cell volumes with both large and small cells showing reduced viability.
evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by single-cell microscopy measurements of septum positioning (Cs) and growth asymmetry (Cg), with data shown in Figure 1G demonstrating the relationship between cell volume and viability. The measurements are quantitative and reproducible.

result: After 1000 generations of experimental evolution, all ten replicate populations rapidly restored fitness to wild-type levels while retaining spherical morphology, with decreased cell volume defining a new phenotype distinct from the ancestral ΔmreB population.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 are supported by fitness measurements at multiple time points (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2), microscopy showing retained spherical shape (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and cell volume measurements. The rapid, parallel fitness restoration across replicates is well-documented.

result: Whole-genome sequencing identified pbp1A mutations in seven of ten evolved lines, with specific mutations D484N (Line 1), D721A (Line 3), T362P (Line 4), and N698K (Line 6), while other lines showed mutations in ftsA (Line 2), ftsZ (Line 5), or a five-gene deletion including oprD (Line 7). All lines had at least one pbp1A mutation by generation 50.
evaluation: Claims C42-C51, C59 are supported by whole-genome sequencing data (Supplementary file 1) and colony sequencing at generation 50 (Supplementary file 2). The identification of specific mutations and their frequencies is well-documented, though the functional significance requires additional validation.

result: The pbp1A gene encodes a class A PBP with both TPase and TGase activities that interacts with the rod complex. Mutations in Lines 1 and 4 target the TPase domain and OB/ODD domain respectively, with similar mutations in other bacteria causing loss-of-function.
evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are supported by protein structure mapping (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), established knowledge about class A PBPs, and citations to relevant literature (Banzhaf et al., 2012; Geisinger et al., 2020; Job et al., 2008; Land and Winkler, 2011; Typas et al., 2011).

result: Genetic reconstruction of pbp1A mutations (D484N and T362P) in the ΔmreB background produces spherical cells with near-ancestral volume and DNA content, restores fitness to wild-type levels, and demonstrates that loss-of-function of pbp1A is sufficient for fitness restoration.
evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by microscopy and flow cytometry (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), fitness assays (Figure 2A), growth curves (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), elongation rate measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), and comparison with ΔmreB Δpbp1A double mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 7). The reconstruction experiments demonstrate causality.

result: When reconstructed in ancestral SBW25, pbp1A mutations have minimal effects on population dynamics and shape but reduce elongation rates and cell width, suggesting reduction or complete loss-of-function with decreased lateral cell wall synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C67-C73 are supported by growth curves (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), microscopy (Figure 2B), elongation rate measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), cell width measurements, and comparisons to similar observations in other bacteria (citations to Murray et al., 1998; Claessen et al., 2008; Kawai et al., 2009; Banzhaf et al., 2012). Claim C73 is appropriately labeled as speculation.

result: The five-gene deletion in Line 7 (including oprD encoding an outer membrane porin) restores fitness in the ΔmreB background but causes extended lag time, incomplete septation, and aberrant growth characteristics when reconstructed in either ΔmreB or wild-type backgrounds.
evaluation: Claims C74-C88 are supported by genome annotation (Figure 2—figure supplement 10, Supplementary file 1), fitness assays (Figure 2A), growth curves (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), microscopy showing incomplete septation (multiple figures), cell volume and DNA content measurements (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and statistical analysis. The complex phenotype is well-characterized.

result: Cell volume homeostasis depends on the balance between turgor pressure and membrane tension. Loss of mreB is expected to decrease internal pressure, and ΔmreB cells show reduced volume in exponential phase compared to stationary phase. Adaptive mutations in evolved lines restored mechanical integrity of the cell wall, with added volumes matching theoretical predictions for spherical geometry.
evaluation: Claims C89-C97 are supported by biophysical principles (citations to Rojas and Huang, 2018; Le Verge-Serandour and Turlier, 2021; Campos et al., 2014; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2017), added volume measurements (Figure 3A), time-lapse microscopy (Video 2), and theoretical calculations. Claims C90, C94 are appropriately labeled as speculation/inference. The biophysical framework is sound.

result: Cell volume homeostasis requires balanced elongation and septation rates. In ΔmreB cells, septation rate significantly exceeds elongation rate, leading to unstable volume distribution and expected volume decrease. Evolved lines and pbp1A reconstructions restored this balance, while the Line 7 deletion did not.
evaluation: Claims C98-C109 are supported by measurements of elongation and septation rates (Figure 3B) and logical principles of cell size homeostasis. The data clearly show imbalance in ΔmreB and restoration in evolved lines. Claims C98-C101, C103-C104, C106, C108 involve appropriate inferences from the data.

result: All evolved lines regained symmetry in elongation rate and septum positioning, with improvement most notable for elongation rate symmetry. This correlates with increased proliferative capacity. Asymmetry in elongation rate has greater impact on cell survival than septum positioning, with probability of passing to next generation decreasing linearly with growth asymmetry up to 50%.
evaluation: Claims C110-C124 are supported by measurements of Cg and Cs (Figure 3C-D), correlation with probability p, and analysis of division time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The data clearly demonstrate that elongation rate symmetry is the primary determinant of fitness restoration. Claims C112, C121, C123-C124 involve appropriate inferences and speculation.

result: Peptidoglycan analysis shows that ΔmreB mutants have increased cross-linking (40.47%) compared to wild-type (36.34%), while pbp1A mutants show reduced cross-linking (31.28-33.66%). Bocillin-FL labeling indicates elevated Pbp1A TPase activity in ΔmreB, with the Line 1 mutation showing little change and Line 4 mutation showing absent signal.
evaluation: Claims C125-C132 are supported by peptidoglycan analysis (Figure 4A) and Bocillin-FL labeling (Figure 4B). The biochemical data are quantitative with appropriate replicates and statistical analysis. Claim C128 is an appropriate inference. The data support the conclusion that pbp1A mutations affect TPase activity.

result: FDAA labeling reveals that wild-type cells show homogeneous cell wall synthesis on lateral surfaces with enrichment at mid-cell during septation, while ΔmreB cells show heterogeneous synthesis across the entire cell wall. This heterogeneity is contrary to observations in E. coli and indicates active but dysregulated cell wall synthesis. pbp1A mutations restore homogeneity by eliminating disorganized synthesis patterns.
evaluation: Claims C133-C138 are supported by FDAA labeling data (Figure 4C) and comparison to published E. coli data (citation to Ursell et al., 2014). The observation of heterogeneous synthesis in ΔmreB P. fluorescens contrasts with E. coli, which is an important finding. Claims C136, C138 are appropriate inferences from the imaging data.

result: Fitness compensation occurred rapidly (by generation 250) through single-step mutations, primarily in pbp1A. All evolved lines retained spherical shape, consistent with evidence that rod-shape cannot be restored without MreB, though rod-shaped bacteria lacking MreB exist in Actinobacteria and Rhizobiales.
evaluation: Claims C139-C145 are supported by fitness measurements (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), sequencing data, reconstruction experiments, microscopy (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and citations to relevant literature (Shi et al., 2018; Margolin, 2009; Zhao et al., 2021). Claim C145 is appropriately labeled as speculation.

result: The most obvious difference between ancestral ΔmreB and evolved lines is cell volume. Viability depends on cell volume in ΔmreB cells, declining in both very large and very small cells. The primary cause of volume variability is differential elongation rate among sister cells (Cg), leading to the prediction that fitness restoration requires mutations restoring homogeneity in elongation rate.
evaluation: Claims C146-C153 are supported by cell volume measurements, viability data (Figure 1G), and analysis of Cs and Cg (Figure 3C-D). The inference that differential elongation rate is the primary cause (C152) and the prediction about fitness restoration (C153) are logical and supported by subsequent experimental results. Claims C149-C150 are appropriately labeled as speculation.

result: ΔmreB cells show increased peptidoglycan cross-linking, enhanced Pbp1A TPase activity, and heterogeneous cell wall synthesis, indicating that cell wall synthesis continues but is dysregulated in the absence of MreB. This contrasts with E. coli. Two hypotheses are proposed: (1) elongasome is non-functional with synthesis by aPBPs, or (2) elongasome remains functional but is stalled due to elevated TPase activity from altered Pbp2-Pbp1A interactions.
evaluation: Claims C154-C169 are supported by peptidoglycan analysis (Figure 4A), Bocillin-FL labeling (Figure 4B), FDAA labeling (Figure 4C), and citations to relevant literature. The presentation of two competing hypotheses is appropriate given the data. Claims C157-C158, C162, C164-C165, C167 are appropriately labeled as speculation or citation-based. The elevated TPase activity in ΔmreB (C169) supports the second hypothesis.

result: Fitness restoration in evolved populations stemmed from reduction or abolition of Pbp1A function, with greatest improvement in elongation rate symmetry (Cg) correlating with increased daughter cell viability. Selection restored fitness by reducing variation in elongation rate among daughter cells, linked to reduced TPase function and peptidoglycan cross-linking favoring disorganized cell wall architecture suited to spherical topology.
evaluation: Claims C170-C175 are supported by sequencing data, reconstruction experiments, measurements of Cg and Cs (Figure 3C-D), correlation with probability p, and biochemical assays (Figure 4A-B). The mechanistic connection between pbp1A mutations, reduced TPase activity, and restored fitness is well-established. Claim C175 is appropriately labeled as speculation but is supported by the data and model (Figure 4D).

result: Two mechanistic explanations for how pbp1A mutations restore fitness are proposed: (1) inactivation of Pbp1A increases Pbp1B activity allowing uniform wall repair, or (2) elimination of Pbp1A corrects the balance between TPase and GTase activity allowing the elongasome to move more diffusively.
evaluation: Claims C176-C178 are appropriately labeled as speculation and are supported by citations to relevant literature (Vigouroux et al., 2020; Simpson et al., 2021). These represent testable hypotheses for future work. The presentation of alternative mechanistic explanations is scientifically appropriate given the current data.

result: The reason ΔmreB cells are viable in SBW25 under standard laboratory conditions is unknown. Deletion of mreB is lethal in many bacteria including P. aeruginosa, though lethality can be rescued by slow growth or increased FtsZ activity in E. coli, or magnesium in B. subtilis. This suggests that viability depends on subtleties in elongasome component interactions.
evaluation: Claims C179-C183 are supported by citations to relevant literature (Robertson et al., 2007; Kruse et al., 2005; Bendezú and de Boer, 2008; Formstone and Errington, 2005). Claim C179 appropriately acknowledges a gap in understanding. Claim C183 is appropriately labeled as speculation about why SBW25 differs from other bacteria.

result: The evolutionary route from rod to sphere is readily achievable under laboratory conditions via mreB loss followed by compensatory pbp1A mutation and peptidoglycan reorganization. Whether this occurs in nature depends on environmental context and initial fitness effects. In Neisseriaceae, the transition may require loss of yacF followed by compensation and eventual elongasome loss.
evaluation: Claims C184-C190 are supported by the experimental results presented in this work and citations to relevant literature (Siefert and Fox, 1998; Veyrier et al., 2015). Claims C189-C190 are appropriately labeled as speculation about evolutionary implications. The comparison to Neisseriaceae provides important context.

result: Cylindrical shape offers advantages over spherical shape including more efficient surface/volume ratio, advantages for surface attachment and biofilm formation, and constant supply/demand ratio during growth. Spherical cells must evolve complex regulatory networks to maintain protein concentrations despite changing surface/volume ratio, while rod-shaped bacteria can use simpler regulatory networks.
evaluation: Claims C191-C199 are supported by geometric and biophysical principles, citations to relevant literature (Young, 2006), and logical inferences about regulatory requirements. Claim C191 is appropriately labeled as speculation. These claims provide important evolutionary context for understanding the significance of the findings.

result: Line 5 contained an ftsZ mutation at generation 500 that was undetected at generation 1000. The same FtsZ D176A mutation was found in a separate selection experiment with ΔrodA. The prevalence of pbp1A mutations likely reflects that loss-of-function mutations are more readily achieved than gain-of-function ftsZ mutations, with all lines carrying at least one pbp1A mutation by generation 50.
evaluation: Claims C200-C204 are supported by sequencing data (Supplementary file 1-2) and unpublished data. The inference about mutational accessibility (C202) is logical and supported by the colony sequencing data at generation 50 (C203). Claim C204 is appropriately labeled as speculation about future research.

result: The Line 7 five-gene deletion likely limits water influx through loss of OprD porin, damping turgor pressure changes and reducing cell swelling. However, this deletion causes incomplete septation in both SBW25 and ΔmreB backgrounds, which was subsequently rescued by mutation in the divisome protein FtsE.
evaluation: Claims C205-C208 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 4C, Figure 2—figure supplement 9), time-lapse microscopy (Video 3), and sequencing data showing the ftsE mutation. Claim C205 is appropriately labeled as speculation about the mechanism. Claim C208 is an inference based on the observed septation defects and presence of the ftsE mutation.
